Q700.L1t: Standing waves in pipes form at frequencies set by the pipe's length and the speed of sound in the air inside it.
Q700.L2t: An open pipe has an antinode of displacement at each end, so it supports every integer multiple of its fundamental frequency.
Q700.L3t: A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental is half the open pipe's, 25 Hz, and only odd multiples of that appear (25, 75, 125, 175, 225 Hz and so on).
Q700.L4t: Once the pipe is closed at one end, none of the original five frequencies is still present.
Q700.L2f: An open pipe supports only the odd-numbered harmonics, because both of its ends must be displacement nodes.
Q700.L3f: Closing one end keeps the open pipe's own frequencies but removes the fundamental and every even-numbered harmonic, leaving the higher odd ones.
Q700.L4f: After closing one end, the higher odd harmonics, 150 Hz and 250 Hz, are the ones that remain.

Q675.L1t: A pair of linear equations in two unknowns can be solved by elimination or by substitution.
Q675.L2t: The coefficients of the two equations are not proportional, so the system has exactly one solution for x and y.
Q675.L3t: Subtracting the first equation from the second gives x + y = 2, and substituting that into the first equation leaves 2y = 50, so y and then x can be found.
Q675.L4t: The difference x - y comes out as a large negative number, equal to negative forty-eight.
Q675.L2f: The two equations are multiples of each other, so the system has infinitely many solutions.
Q675.L3f: Subtracting the first equation from the second gives 4x + 4y = 8, which shows directly that x - y equals 8 divided by 4.
Q675.L4f: The value of x - y is positive two.

Q652.L1t: An argument is valid only if no assignment of truth values makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q652.L2t: An indirect truth table assumes the premises are true and the conclusion false, then checks whether those assumptions can be held consistently.
Q652.L3t: For the conclusion to be false, L and R must be true and P false; the third premise then forces Q false, which makes the consequent of the second premise false, so N must be true and O false to keep that premise true.
Q652.L4t: The argument is invalid, because the premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
Q652.L2f: An indirect truth table shows an argument is invalid when assuming true premises and a true conclusion produces consistent values.
Q652.L3f: When L and R are true and P is false, the third premise forces Q to be true, which makes the second premise's consequent true and so blocks any way of falsifying the conclusion.
Q652.L4f: The argument is valid, because no assignment makes all the premises true and the conclusion false.
